summary: Describes the Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support protocol, which lets an entire mobile network attach to different points in the Internet. It extends Mobile IPv6 so that every node in the moving network keeps its sessions and stays reachable, with a Mobile Router connecting the network to the outside.

eli5.summary: When a whole bus full of passengers drives across town, the bus keeps one internet connection for everyone and keeps it working as it moves.

questions: how does nemo basic support work
what is the mobile router flag in binding update
subtitle: How a whole moving network, such as the network on a vehicle, keeps its addresses and sessions by tunneling through a home agent.

tldr.problem: When an entire network moves and attaches to different points in the Internet, every node inside it should keep its sessions and stay reachable, without any of those nodes having to know about the movement.
tldr.mechanism: NEMO Basic Support extends Mobile IPv6. A Mobile Router registers its current location with its Home Agent using a Binding Update with a new R flag, and a bi-directional tunnel carries all traffic for the Mobile Network between the two.
tldr.outcome: Network mobility is transparent to the nodes inside the Mobile Network. The cost is that all traffic passes through the Home Agent, because this document does not describe route optimization.

today: RFC 3963 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Moving a Whole Network
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support adds protocol extensions to Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) so that an entire network can move. The extensions are backward compatible with Mobile IPv6: a NEMO-compliant Home Agent can still operate as a Mobile IPv6 Home Agent.

The goal is session continuity for every node in the Mobile Network as its Mobile Router changes its point of attachment to the Internet, plus continued reachability of those nodes. The Mobile Network may hold nodes that support mobility and nodes that do not.

The RFC states its limits openly. All traffic between nodes in the Mobile Network and Correspondent Nodes passes through the Home Agent, and route optimization of this traffic is not described. Multihoming for Mobile Routers is not discussed either. Nested mobility, where one Mobile Router attaches to the Mobile Network of another, is allowed with no limit on the levels, but each level adds another IPv6 header encapsulation to data packets.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school bus where every kid has a phone. NEMO lets the bus carry one shared connection so every kid's phone keeps working while the bus drives around.

sections.title: How NEMO Works
sections.content:
A Mobile Network is a subnet that can attach to arbitrary points in the routing infrastructure. It is reached only through a Mobile Router, which is also the default gateway for the network. The Mobile Router does not announce the Mobile Network routes where it is currently attached. Instead it keeps a bi-directional tunnel to its Home Agent, which advertises an aggregation of Mobile Networks to the infrastructure.

When the Mobile Router gets a Care-of Address on a visited link, it immediately sends a Binding Update to its Home Agent. To act as a router and not only as a mobile host, it sets the new Mobile Router flag (R). It may also say which Mobile Network Prefixes it serves. The Home Agent answers with a Binding Acknowledgement, and a positive answer with R set means forwarding for the Mobile Network is in place.

From then on, packets from the Mobile Network with a source address in the Mobile Network Prefix are reverse-tunneled to the Home Agent using IP-in-IP encapsulation, and the Home Agent decapsulates them and forwards them to the Correspondent Node. Packets sent to the Mobile Network arrive at the Home Agent, which tunnels them to the Mobile Router's current Care-of Address. The Mobile Router checks that the outer source is the Home Agent (unless IPsec tunnel mode protects the packet) and that the inner destination belongs to a Mobile Network prefix, and otherwise should drop the packet.

Mobile Nodes that attach to the Mobile Network treat it as a normal IPv6 access network and run Mobile IPv6 as usual.
sections.eli5: The bus has a driver who always phones the school office to say where the bus is now. Letters for the kids go to the office first, and the office sends them on to wherever the bus is.

sections.title: Message Changes
sections.content:
The protocol changes few things on the wire. The Binding Update gains a Mobile Router flag (R). If it is 0, the Home Agent treats the sender as a plain mobile node and MUST NOT forward packets for the Mobile Network to it. The Binding Acknowledgement gains the same flag, which is set only if the matching Binding Update had it set to 1, and which tells the Mobile Router that the Home Agent supports Mobile Routers.

A new mobility option, the Mobile Network Prefix Option, carries one prefix. It has type 6, its Length is set to 18, it has a Reserved byte (zero on send, ignored on receipt), a Prefix Length and a sixteen-byte prefix. A Binding Update may carry several of these options, one per prefix.

Four new Binding Acknowledgement status values are defined, listed in the table below. Values below 128 mean the Binding Update was processed successfully, and the higher values mean the Home Agent rejected it.
sections.eli5: NEMO adds a tick box on the letter that says "I am a whole bus, not just one kid", and a way to list which seat rows belong to the bus.

sections.title: What the Mobile Router Does
sections.content:
A Mobile Router combines the behavior of a host, a router and a Mobile IPv6 mobile node. It MUST implement everything required of IPv6 mobile nodes. It uses one of two ways to tell the Home Agent which prefixes are its own, and sets R in both:

  • Implicit mode: no Mobile Network Prefix Option is sent. The Home Agent finds the prefixes by some other means, for example manual configuration.
  • Explicit mode: the Binding Update carries one or more Mobile Network Prefix Options, including in refreshes of an existing binding.

A Mobile Router MUST implement at least one mode and MAY implement both. If R is set, the Home Registration flag (H) MUST be set too.

If the acknowledgement lacks R, the Mobile Router concludes its Home Agent does not support Mobile Routers, MUST de-register, and repeats Dynamic Home Agent Address Discovery to find one that does. For the new error statuses 140 to 143, the Mobile Router generally SHOULD try another Home Agent on the home link. If none answers positively, it stops sending Binding Updates with R set for that Home Address, and for status 140 it MUST log the information.

On a visited link, the Mobile Router SHOULD NOT send unsolicited Router Advertisements or answer Router Solicitations on its egress interface, but it MUST NOT ignore Router Advertisements received there. When it detects that it is back home, it MUST de-register.
sections.eli5: The bus driver has two ways to tell the office which seats are on the bus: let the office already know, or read the list out loud every time. If one office says no, the driver tries another office.

sections.title: What the Home Agent Does
sections.content:
A Home Agent that serves Mobile Routers MUST satisfy the Mobile IPv6 Home Agent requirements and MUST implement both the implicit and explicit modes. When it gets a Binding Update with R set, it checks that the H flag is set, or else rejects it with status 140. It rejects a change of the R value on an existing binding with status 139.

In explicit mode it MUST set up forwarding for all prefixes listed, and if it cannot set up all of them it MUST NOT forward for any and rejects the update with status 141. It SHOULD keep a Prefix Table, indexed by the Mobile Router's Home Address, to stop a router claiming prefixes that belong to another; a failed check gives status 142. In implicit mode with no usable configured information, it rejects with status 143.

If all checks pass, the Home Agent creates or updates the binding cache entry, defends the Home Address with Proxy Neighbor Discovery and sets up the tunnel. Data for the Mobile Network MUST be forwarded through the tunnel, using the routing table, the binding cache or both. On de-registration it removes the binding, the tunnel and the Mobile Network routes.

Dynamic Home Agent Address Discovery is extended with a new R flag in the request, the reply and the Home Agent Information Option, so Mobile Routers can find Home Agents that support them.
sections.eli5: The school office keeps a list of which seat rows belong to which bus. If a bus claims rows that belong to another bus, the office says no.

sections.title: Running a Routing Protocol Through the Tunnel
sections.content:
Instead of using prefixes in Binding Updates, the Mobile Router and Home Agent may run an intra-domain routing protocol such as RIPng or OSPF through the bi-directional tunnel. This is optional and governed by configuration. The RFC calls it very useful when the Mobile Network is large with many subnets, because routing changes propagate quickly in both directions.

While away from home, the Mobile Router should stop sending routing updates on its visited-link interface, which reduces the chance that Mobile Network prefixes leak to the visited network. The tunnel is treated as a tunnel interface. When a routing protocol is used, the Mobile Router SHOULD NOT include prefixes in the Binding Update, since that would be redundant.

Routing messages from the Home Agent could reveal the home network's internal structure, so they require authentication and confidentiality protection, and the OSPFv3 mechanisms the RFC points to MUST be used. Appendix B adds advice for link state protocols: keep one tunnel interface per Mobile Router instead of tearing it down at every move, treat it as an on-demand circuit for OSPF, and do not configure the entire home domain as a single OSPF area.
sections.eli5: For a very big bus fleet, the buses and the office can just keep telling each other the road map directly, instead of listing seats on every letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All signaling between the Mobile Router and the Home Agent MUST be authenticated by IPsec, as for Mobile IPv6 in RFC 3776. The NEMO messages extend Mobile IPv6 messages and need no changes to that protection.

The tunnel could let nodes in the Mobile Network spoof addresses, so checks are required at both ends. The Mobile Router SHOULD ingress-filter packets from the Mobile Network, checking that source addresses belong to the Mobile Network Prefix and are not addresses of the Mobile Router itself. The Home Agent MUST verify that tunneled packets have the Mobile Router's Care-of Address as outer source and an inner source that is topologically correct for the Mobile Network prefixes.

If a Binding Update carries prefix options, the Home Agent MUST be able to verify that the router is authorized for them before it sets up forwarding. Routing protocol messages need confidentiality protection, which IPsec ESP in tunnel mode over the whole tunnel already provides.
sections.eli5: The driver and the office must prove who they are, and both check that nobody on the bus is putting a fake return address on a letter.

messages.label: Binding Update (R set)
messages.note: Sent once a Care-of Address is acquired; may carry Mobile Network Prefix Options.

messages.label: Binding Acknowledgement (R set)
messages.note: Status 0 means forwarding for the Mobile Network is set up.

messages.label: Packet for a Mobile Network node
messages.note: Routed to the Home Agent that holds the binding.

messages.label: Tunneled packet
messages.note: Sent to the Care-of Address; the Mobile Router decapsulates it.

messages.label: Reverse-tunneled reply
messages.note: IP-in-IP; the Home Agent forwards it to the Correspondent Node.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of the option, excluding the type and length fields.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Initialized to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Length of the IPv6 prefix in the option.

fields.name: Mobile Network Prefix
fields.desc: A sixteen-byte field holding the prefix.

items.label: Mobile Router Operation not permitted
items.desc: The Home Agent is not configured for Mobile Routers, or H was not set.

items.label: Invalid Prefix
items.desc: Forwarding could not be set up for one or more prefixes.

items.label: Forwarding Setup failed (prefixes missing)
items.desc: No usable prefix information; used in implicit mode.
